common_name: Zuni Gold Bean (Pueblo Heirloom Golden Dry Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost once soil warms above 65°F; Zuni Gold is a Native American heirloom dry bean from Zuni Pueblo in New Mexico.

directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm soil after last frost, spacing 4-6 inches apart in rows. Zuni Gold is a Native American heirloom bush dry bean traditionally grown at Zuni Pueblo in the arid high desert of New Mexico, its smooth, golden-yellow seeds cooking up creamy with a mild, buttery flavor prized in traditional Zuni and Southwestern cooking. Adapted over generations to the low rainfall and short growing season of the Southwest, it tolerates dry conditions better than many bean varieties bred for wetter climates. Allow pods to dry fully on the plant before harvesting for storage as a dry bean.

common_name: Tohono O'odham 60-Day Corn (Desert-Adapted Sonoran Flour Corn)

planting.note: Direct sow after soil is reliably warm; Tohono O'odham 60-Day Corn was bred by the Tohono O'odham people of the Sonoran Desert to mature quickly, ahead of the end of the summer monsoon season.

directions: Direct sow in warm, well-drained soil in full sun, planting in blocks rather than single rows to ensure good pollination. Tohono O'odham 60-Day Corn is a remarkably fast-maturing flour corn developed by the Tohono O'odham people of the Sonoran Desert of Arizona and Sonora, bred to reach maturity in about two months so a crop could be planted and harvested within the brief window of the summer monsoon rains. Its speed and drought adaptation make it valuable for short-season gardens or a fast succession planting anywhere. Harvest and dry ears fully before grinding the kernels into flour for traditional dishes like pinole and tortillas.

common_name: Cherokee Long Greasy Bean (Shiny-Podded Appalachian Heirloom Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost once soil warms above 60°F; greasy beans get their name from smooth, glossy pods that lack the fuzzy texture of most snap beans.

directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm soil after last frost, spacing 6-9 inches apart along a trellis or corn stalks. Cherokee Long Greasy is one of many named greasy bean varieties preserved within Cherokee communities of the Southern Appalachians, its pods smooth and shiny rather than fuzzy, a trait that gives the whole greasy bean class its name, with tender, flavorful pods good for snapping and flavorful seeds that also dry well for winter storage. It reflects a long tradition of bean cultivation and seed saving among Cherokee gardeners in the mountains of western North Carolina, Tennessee, and Georgia. Harvest young for snap beans or let pods dry fully on the vine for a dry bean crop.

common_name: Ayocote Negro Bean (Black Mexican Runner Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with a sturdy trellis; Ayocote Negro is a large-seeded black Mexican runner bean, a staple of central Mexican cooking.

directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm soil after last frost, providing a sturdy trellis or pole for the vigorous vines to climb. Ayocote Negro bears large, glossy black seeds inside long runner bean pods, a traditional Mexican dry bean valued for its meaty texture and rich, earthy flavor in stews and slow-cooked dishes, distinct from the smaller common bean species most Americans grow. As a runner bean it produces attractive clusters of flowers that also draw hummingbirds before setting pods, making it ornamental as well as productive. Allow pods to dry fully on the vine before shelling for storage.

common_name: Chapalote Corn (Ancient Mexican Popcorn-Type Flint Corn)

planting.note: Direct sow after soil is reliably warm; Chapalote is among the oldest surviving Mexican corn varieties, a popcorn-textured flint type grown for centuries in Sinaloa.

directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, planting in blocks rather than single rows to ensure good pollination. Chapalote is one of the oldest documented corn varieties still cultivated in the Americas, a tall, dark-kerneled flint corn from the coastal state of Sinaloa in northwestern Mexico with a distinctive popcorn-like kernel texture that connects it to some of the earliest domesticated maize lineages. It is used both for pinole (roasted, ground corn) and as a genuinely popping corn, reflecting its ancient, less fully domesticated kernel structure. Harvest and dry ears fully before shelling and storing kernels.
sources: Slow Food Foundation — Ark of Taste

common_name: Pasilla de Oaxaca Pepper (Smoke-Dried Oaxacan Chile)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; Pasilla de Oaxaca is traditionally wood-smoked and dried, distinct from the standard pasilla (chile negro) pepper used elsewhere in Mexico.

directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into rich, well-drained soil in full sun. Pasilla de Oaxaca produces elongated, dark green pods that ripen to deep red-brown and are traditionally cured over wood smoke before drying, a regional Oaxacan specialty distinct from the standard pasilla (chile negro) grown elsewhere in Mexico and prized in stews and moles for its smoky, fruity heat. The plants bear well over a long warm season in a climate similar to their native highland Oaxacan growing region. Harvest pods once fully colored for drying and smoking, or use fresh while still green.
sources: Slow Food Foundation — Ark of Taste

common_name: Chile de Agua (Fresh Oaxacan Valley Pepper)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; Chile de Agua is a fresh green pepper of Oaxaca's central valleys, used widely for rajas and stuffed chile dishes.

directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into rich, well-drained soil in full sun. Chile de Agua produces medium-to-large, tapered, pale to medium green pods with mild-to-moderate heat, a defining fresh chile of Oaxaca's central valleys used widely for roasted rajas (strips) and stuffed chile dishes in Oaxacan cuisine. The productive plants perform well over a long warm season, and pods are typically harvested and used green rather than allowed to ripen to red. Harvest regularly to encourage continued production through the summer.
sources: Slow Food Foundation — Ark of Taste

common_name: Greasy Cutshort Bean (Tightly-Packed Appalachian Heirloom Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost once soil warms above 60°F; cutshort beans get their name from seeds packed so tightly inside the pod that the pod tip appears squared off.

directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm soil after last frost, spacing 6-9 inches apart along a trellis or corn stalks. Greasy Cutshort combines two classic Appalachian heirloom bean traits in one variety: smooth, shiny, fuzz-free 'greasy' pods, and seeds packed so densely inside each pod that the tip is squared off rather than tapered, the 'cutshort' trait long selected for by mountain gardeners saving their own seed. The tender pods are good for snapping young, and the beans shell out well for a flavorful dry bean later in the season. Allow some pods to dry fully on the vine each year to save seed and maintain the strain.

planting.note: Plant certified seed pieces after soil has warmed slightly; Vitelotte Noire is a French heirloom fingerling with deep purple skin and flesh, also called 'Truffe de Chine.'

directions: Plant certified seed pieces 3-4 inches deep in light, well-drained soil; as a late-maturing fingerling it needs a full season to size up its knobby tubers. Vitelotte Noire is a classic French heirloom potato with deep purple skin and equally deep purple flesh throughout, nicknamed 'Truffe de Chine' (Chinese truffle) for its dark, irregular tuber shape, and prized by chefs for the striking color it brings to gratins, chips, and purées without losing much pigment when cooked. Its dense, nutty flavor and firm texture hold up well in roasted and sautéed preparations. Harvest once foliage yellows and dies back, and cure tubers in a cool, dark spot before storage.

common_name: Bonnotte Potato (Early French Island New Potato)

planting.note: Plant certified seed pieces after soil has warmed slightly; Bonnotte is a prized early French new potato traditionally hand-harvested on the island of Noirmoutier.

directions: Plant certified seed pieces 3-4 inches deep in light, well-drained, sandy soil; Bonnotte is an early-maturing variety best harvested young as a thin-skinned new potato rather than left to mature fully. Bonnotte is celebrated in France as one of the earliest and most prized new potatoes, traditionally hand-harvested on the sandy, salt-influenced soils of the Île de Noirmoutier off the Atlantic coast, prized for delicate, thin skin and sweet, buttery flesh that needs little more than a quick steam and butter to shine. Harvest young, while the skin still rubs off easily, for the best texture and flavor, and use promptly since new potatoes do not store as long as mature ones.
sources: Slow Food Foundation — Ark of Taste

common_name: Camus de Bretagne Artichoke (Large Round Breton Artichoke)
scientific_name: Cynara cardunculus var. scolymus 'Camus de Bretagne'

planting.note: Transplant after last frost into deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Camus de Bretagne is the classic large, rounded artichoke of Brittany, France, holding Protected Geographical Indication status there.

directions: Transplant into deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, working in plenty of compost before planting. Camus de Bretagne produces very large, rounded, tightly closed globe artichokes with a pale green color and tender, meaty heart, the classic variety grown in Brittany, France, where it holds Protected Geographical Indication status and accounts for the majority of French artichoke production. Like other globe artichokes it is a true perennial in mild-winter climates, though it can be grown as an annual from an early start in colder zones. Harvest buds while still tightly closed, before the scales begin to loosen, for the best eating quality.
sources: Slow Food Foundation — Ark of Taste

common_name: Ormskirk Late Cabbage (Lancashire Winter Savoy Cabbage)

planting.note: Start seed in late summer for transplanting out for a winter harvest, or start in early spring for fall harvest; Ormskirk Late is a very cold-hardy Savoy-type winter cabbage from Lancashire, England.

directions: Start seed in a nursery bed or trays and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, timing planting so heads mature through the cool season. Ormskirk Late is a traditional Savoy-type winter cabbage bred in the town of Ormskirk in Lancashire, England, valued for its deeply crinkled, dark blue-green leaves and dense, sweet-flavored heads that improve in flavor after exposure to frost, and for standing in the garden through hard winter weather without splitting. It is well suited to a long, cool fall-to-winter growing season in mild climates like the Gulf South. Harvest heads once firm, cutting at the base and leaving the outer wrapper leaves in the garden.

common_name: Nothstine Dent Corn (Wisconsin Yellow Dent Heirloom Corn)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; Nothstine Dent is a Wisconsin farm-family heirloom yellow dent corn preserved through the Seed Savers Exchange.

directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, planting in blocks rather than single rows to ensure good pollination. Nothstine Dent is a Wisconsin heirloom yellow dent corn passed down within a single farm family for generations before being preserved and distributed through the Seed Savers Exchange, valued for reliable yields of good-quality meal and feed corn adapted to short-season Upper Midwest growing conditions. Its relatively short season to maturity makes it a practical choice for regions with a shorter frost-free window than the Gulf South typically has. Harvest and dry ears fully before shelling and storing kernels for grinding or seed.
